source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks, Cognitive Science 18
finding: Tower of Hanoi isomorphs with identical formal structure differed in difficulty depending on how many rules were put into the external display (physical constraints) instead of memory. The more rules were external, the easier the problem.
numbers: Exp 1B (cup-style isomorphs, 18 students): ordering by times, steps and errors was consistent; all errors were on internal rules, none on external rules. Exp 2 used 24 students; Exp 3 used 36 students on nine dimension isomorphs (ordinal and nominal dimensions).
quote: the more rules externalized, the easier the problem. In addition, external rules seem to be error proof
limits: Small student samples (18, 24, 36), one puzzle family, lab task with no real stakes. Some pairwise differences were not significant (for example II-E3 vs II-E23). Counterbalancing of start and end positions was not possible. Numbers read from OCR-garbled PDF.
agent_relevance: A rule held in the interface or enforced by code cannot be broken. A rule held only in the model's prompt can. Put hard rules in code checks, not in prose.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
finding: Interface design alone changed agent success on the same model. A custom agent-computer interface (file viewer, edit command, search, linter) beat a plain shell.
numbers: SWE-bench pass@1 12.5% and HumanEvalFix 87.7% with GPT-4 Turbo. Table 3 on SWE-bench Lite: edit with linting 18.0%, edit without linting 15.0% (-3.0), no edit command 10.3% (-7.7).
quote: significantly enhances an agent's ability to create and edit code files, navigate entire repositories, and execute tests
limits: Ablations on SWE-bench Lite (300 tasks), one model in the ablation, single runs so gaps of a few points may be noise. Absolute scores are from 2024 models and are now far exceeded.
agent_relevance: Guardrail-style feedback at the edit step (linter) paid off. Our edit and check interface for the model is a measurable lever, not decoration.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent, search and viewer ablations
finding: More interface is not always better. Iterative search (next/prev through results) was worse than no search tool, because agents read every match. Summarized search was best. A 100-line file window beat both 30 lines and the full file.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: summarized search 18.0%, no search 15.7%, iterative search 12.0%. File viewer: 30 lines 14.3%, 100 lines 18.0%, full file 12.7%. Context: last 5 observations 18.0%, full history 15.0%.
limits: Single benchmark, single model, small gaps (2-6 points) with no confidence intervals reported in the table. Authors tuned the default design on this data.
agent_relevance: Tool output length and shape matter. Cap what the model sees per call and summarize. Tools that tempt exhaustive looping can hurt.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: Rival to the interface-heavy agent view. A fixed three-phase pipeline with no agent tool loop (localize, repair, validate) matched or beat open-source agents at far lower cost on SWE-bench Lite.
numbers: GPT-4: 96 of 300 fixed (32.00%), cost $0.70 per issue. Agent-style systems in the same table cost more and scored lower among open-source.
limits: SWE-bench Lite only, 2024. Later agent systems passed it. Benchmark contamination and weak patch checking are known issues for SWE-bench.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation for b02: code-controlled structure can beat a freer tool interface. This matches our rule that the program decides transitions and the model fills slots.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents (CodeAct)
finding: Letting the model emit Python as its action space beat JSON or text tool calls on API-Bank and a new benchmark across 17 LLMs, because code can compose several tools and reuse variables.
numbers: Up to 20% absolute higher success rate and up to 30% fewer actions than JSON/text action formats (17 LLMs).
limits: Abstract-level headline figures. Gains are largest for strong models and wider with model strength; weaker models gain little. Needs a code sandbox.
agent_relevance: The action format is a cognitive artifact. Code as action offloads composition and bookkeeping to an interpreter, but adds a sandbox and safety surface.

source: Tam et al. (2024) Let Me Speak Freely? Impact of Format Restrictions on LLM Performance
finding: Forcing structured output (JSON, XML, YAML) lowered reasoning accuracy, more so for stricter formats. Classification tasks were helped or unchanged.
numbers: gpt-4o-mini (Table 2): GSM8K natural language 94.57, format-restricting instructions 87.17, JSON-mode 86.95, JSON-schema 91.71. Shuffled Objects 82.85 / 81.46 / 76.43 / 81.77. Last Letter 83.11 / 84.73 / 76.00 / 86.07 (JSON-schema beat NL there).
quote: we observe a significant decline in LLMs' reasoning abilities under format restrictions
limits: Effect depends on task, model and prompt wording; standard deviations over 9 prompts are large (up to 9.7). A public rebuttal from a structured-output vendor argued the prompts were weak (not verified here).
agent_relevance: The output format is an interface cost. Let the model reason in free text and extract the answer with code in a separate step.

source: Sclar et al. (2023/2024) Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design
finding: Meaningless formatting changes (separators, casing, spacing) changed accuracy a lot, even with a bigger model, more shots or instruction tuning.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points between equivalent formats on LLaMA-2-13B; about 10 points on average over 50+ tasks and several models; GPT-3.5 up to 56 points over 320 formats, median spread 6.4.
limits: Few-shot classification-style tasks, mostly open models. Instruction-tuned and newer models are less brittle but not immune.
agent_relevance: The prompt layout the code hands the model is part of the interface. Fix one format, test alternatives, and never compare two arms with different layouts.

source: Hsieh et al. (2023) Tool Documentation Enables Zero-Shot Tool-Usage with Large Language Models
finding: With a large set of unfamiliar tools (200 commands), a documentation entry per tool beat few-shot demonstrations. Adding demos on top of docs did not help.
numbers: LLM Cloud CLI, F1 over 50 examples: text-davinci-002 zero-shot 0.02, best few-shot no docs 0.05, docs only 0.37, docs plus demos about 0.35. gpt-3.5-turbo zero-shot 0.13, best few-shot 0.19, docs only 0.45, docs plus demos 0.42-0.44.
limits: Only 50 test examples, 2023 models, tools invented by the authors. On familiar benchmarks (ScienceQA, TabMWP) docs and demos were on par.
agent_relevance: Write precise tool descriptions instead of long examples. A short, exact spec of each operator is the cheap fix.

source: Jin et al. (2025) RAG-MCP: Mitigating Prompt Bloat in LLM Tool Selection via RAG
finding: Giving the model every tool description hurt selection. Retrieving only the relevant tool first raised selection accuracy and cut prompt tokens.
numbers: Tool selection accuracy 43.13% with retrieval vs 18.20% (actual match) and 13.62% (all tools in prompt). Average prompt tokens 1084 with retrieval vs 2133.84 baseline.
limits: Small preprint, one benchmark built by the authors, accuracy falls as the tool pool grows even with retrieval. Weak evidence; treat as a hint.
agent_relevance: Show the model only the operators allowed in the current state. Our state machine already does this; this is a small outside support.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts, TACL
finding: Accuracy depended on where the relevant item sat in the context: best at start or end, worst in the middle, even for long-context models. Extended-context versions were not better at using context.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo multi-document QA: closed-book 56.1%, oracle 88.3%. With 20 documents and the answer in the middle, accuracy fell below the closed-book 56.1%.
quote: performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context
limits: 2023 models. Newer models show a smaller but real position effect in later tests (not read here).
agent_relevance: What the code puts into the context, and in what order, is part of the interface. Put the failing output and the task at the edges, not buried.

source: Nye et al. (2021) Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation with Language Models
finding: An external, written working area (scratchpad) let transformers do multi-step addition and program tracing that direct answering could not, and it helped out-of-distribution lengths.
numbers: Models trained on 1-8 digit addition; scratchpad models generalized to 9 and 10 digits where direct models did not (Fig. 3, read from plots, no exact values captured here).
limits: Needs training or fine-tuning on scratchpad data in the main experiments; few-shot scratchpad on large models was weaker. Digit-addition is a toy.
agent_relevance: The model's written steps are its cognitive artifact, as with pen and paper for people. Visible intermediate state beats hidden computation.

source: Gao et al. (2023) PAL: Program-aided Language Models
finding: Offloading the calculation step to a Python interpreter, leaving the model only the decomposition, beat chain-of-thought, and the gap grew when numbers were large.
numbers: GSM8K: about +15 points absolute over PaLM-540B chain-of-thought (PAL with Codex 72.0). GSM-HARD (large numbers): about +40 points absolute over chain-of-thought (PAL 61.2 vs CoT about 23).
limits: Table text garbled in extraction; figures taken from abstract and table. Part of the gain is Codex being a code model (CoT also improved with Codex). Fits arithmetic-like tasks, not open reasoning.
agent_relevance: Strongest LLM analogue of cognitive offloading: let code do counting and calculation. This supports our rule that the program counts and compares.

source: Yao et al. (2023) ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
finding: Interleaving reasoning with tool calls (search) cut hallucination relative to reasoning alone, but acting-only and reasoning-only each did worse than the mix, and the best system combined ReAct with chain-of-thought self-consistency.
numbers: PaLM-540B HotpotQA exact match: standard 28.7, CoT 29.4, Act 25.7, ReAct 27.4, CoT-SC 33.4, ReAct to CoT-SC 35.1 (best). FEVER accuracy: CoT 56.3, ReAct 60.9. ALFWorld +34 and WebShop +10 absolute success vs imitation/RL baselines.
limits: On HotpotQA, ReAct alone was worse than CoT (27.4 vs 29.4). Tool search returning poor results derailed reasoning. Few-shot prompts hand-written.
agent_relevance: Tools help when their output is checked and combined with reasoning; a tool loop alone is not a gain. Table order is garbled by extraction, check against paper before citing exact cells.

source: Yao et al. (2024) tau-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction
finding: Even strong function-calling agents fail often and inconsistently when they must use tools and follow domain rules with a simulated user. Reliability drops fast across repeated trials.
numbers: gpt-4o pass^1 61% retail and 35% airline; pass^8 below 25% in retail; under 50% of tasks solved overall.
limits: Two domains, simulated user, 2024 models. Newer models score higher on pass^1.
agent_relevance: One good run proves little. Repeat and test consistency. The tool surface does not make the model rule-following; code must enforce policy.

source: Patil et al. (2023) Gorilla: LLM Connected with Massive APIs
finding: GPT-4 hallucinated wrong API usage and wrong arguments. A fine-tuned model plus a document retriever beat GPT-4 on API call writing and handled documentation changes at test time.
numbers: Abstract states Gorilla surpasses GPT-4 on writing API calls on APIBench (HuggingFace, TorchHub, TensorHub); exact accuracies not captured in this pass.
limits: Fine-tuning route, not scaffold. 2023 baselines.
agent_relevance: Argument errors are a common tool failure; validate arguments in code and return the error to the model.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing
finding: Essay writing with an LLM gave weaker neural connectivity, lower ownership and worse recall of own text than search or no tool. Removing the LLM in session 4 left impaired performance.
numbers: 54 participants in sessions 1-3, 18 in session 4. In session 4, LLM-to-Brain group: 78% could not quote anything from their essay and 11% quoted correctly, vs 11% and 78% in Brain-only.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed. 18 per group, only 18 in the crossover session, EEG with many comparisons, AI-judge scoring, and a self-selected sample. Authors warn against strong causal reading.
agent_relevance: Human-side risk, not an agent result. For our agent, the parallel is that the model may do worse once a helper is removed, so test ablations.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science 2010-2015, via FORRT replication atlas
finding: The FORRT atlas records one replication of Sparrow, Liu & Wegner (2011) Google effects on memory, and it failed. The atlas page itself gives only the outcome label.
numbers: 1 replication attempt on record: failed (atlas page). Overall figures (13 of 21 replicated, effect sizes about half of the originals) come from search-result text, not from the paper.
limits: Only the atlas page was read, not the Nature Human Behaviour paper. The original authors disputed the replication design (the 2006 computer words were said to be outdated), per search summary.
agent_relevance: The famous 'Google makes us offload memory' result is weak. Do not build the schema on it.

source: Ruiz Pardo & Minda (2022) Reexamining the brain drain effect: replication of Ward et al. (2017), Acta Psychologica 230
finding: Pre-registered direct replication of Ward et al. Exp 2 (phone on desk, in bag, outside room; on or off, six conditions) found no difference in working-memory span or go/no-go performance by phone location.
numbers: Six conditions, OSpan and Go/No-Go; sample N about 383 per secondary report, not confirmed in abstract.
quote: the mere presence of one's smartphone may not be enough to affect cognitive performance
limits: Abstract only. Single replication of one experiment of the original. Meta-analysis (b19) is mixed.
agent_relevance: The idea that a tool in view drains capacity did not hold in a clean replication. Do not cut tools out on that ground.

source: Boettger, Poschik & Zierer (2023) Does the Brain Drain Effect Really Exist? A Meta-Analysis, Behavioral Sciences 13
finding: Pooled over studies of smartphone use or presence, the overall effect on cognition was negative, but domains differed (memory, attention, general performance), heterogeneity was high, and study origin or nationality mattered.
numbers: 22 studies, 43 effects. Pooled size not captured in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Mixes use with mere presence, so it does not rescue the presence-only claim. Publication bias handling not read.
agent_relevance: Distraction from active use is plausible; passive presence is not. In the agent, noise in the context is the analogue of active use.

source: Urry et al. (2021) Don't Ditch the Laptop Just Yet: direct replication of Mueller & Oppenheimer (2014) Study 1, Psychological Science 32
finding: Laptop notes were longer and more verbatim, as in the original. But laptop users did not do worse on the quiz. The claim that longhand improves encoding was not supported.
numbers: Laptop n=74, longhand n=68. Mini meta-analyses of eight similar studies echoed the pattern. Higher word count tied to better quiz score; verbatim overlap tied to worse score, not robust in replication.
limits: Immediate test only, no study time. Original effect was about conceptual questions after a delay in some studies. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: A tool changes the process (verbatim copying) more reliably than the outcome. Measure outcome, not just process traces.

source: Dahmani & Bohbot (2020) Habitual use of GPS negatively impacts spatial memory during self-guided navigation, Scientific Reports 10
finding: Greater lifetime GPS use went with worse self-guided spatial memory. In 13 retested people, more GPS use over three years went with steeper decline.
numbers: 50 regular drivers cross-sectional; 13 retested after 3 years.
limits: Correlational. Longitudinal sample tiny (13). Self-selection is not fully ruled out, though GPS users did not report a worse sense of direction. Not replicated at scale in what I read.
agent_relevance: Offloading can weaken the offloaded skill. For a fixed model there is no skill to lose, but a fine-tuned or memory-using agent might.

source: Fisher, Goddu & Keil (2015) Searching for explanations: how the Internet inflates estimates of internal knowledge, JEP: General 144
finding: After searching the web for explanations, people rated their own knowledge higher and mistook access for understanding. Held across 9 experiments.
numbers: 9 experiments; effect sizes not in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Self-ratings, not performance. Not checked here against a large-scale replication.
agent_relevance: Tool access inflates confidence. In the agent, tool or retrieval output can raise confidence without raising correctness, so confidence must come from checks.

source: Risko & Gilbert (2016) Cognitive Offloading, Trends in Cognitive Sciences 20
finding: Review of what triggers offloading and what it costs or gains. Offers a metacognitive framework: people offload based on their own estimate of memory ability and task demand.
numbers: No pooled effect; narrative review.
limits: Abstract only. Review written before the 2018-2022 replication wave on Google and smartphone effects.
agent_relevance: Offloading is chosen by self-assessed confidence. If the model's self-assessment is poor, let code decide when to use the tool.

source: Buchli & Storm (2025) Working memory capacity and the saving-enhanced memory effect, Memory 33
finding: Saving earlier material (Storm & Stone 2015) frees capacity for new learning, and people with higher working-memory capacity benefit more. Moderator found in three experiments.
numbers: Three experiments, positive correlation between WM capacity and size of the saving benefit; r not in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Word-list tasks. The original Storm & Stone 2015 effect was not opened.
agent_relevance: Offloading helps most for agents or people who can use the freed capacity. Saved state must be reloadable, not just stored.

source: Hutchins (1995) Cognition in the Wild; Norman (1991) Cognitive artifacts
finding: Founding view: tools do not amplify the person but change the task the person faces. Ship navigation is done by a team plus instruments (not opened this session; recalled).
numbers: No experimental numbers. Ethnographic case.
limits: Not opened. Case study of one Navy ship, no controls. Cited as theory, not as tested effect.
agent_relevance: Our code plus model is the unit being studied, not the model alone. Evaluate the system.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action, Cognitive Science 18
finding: Expert Tetris players rotate pieces on screen to see their fit, not only to place them. Physical action simplifies thinking (epistemic action). Recalled, not opened this session.
numbers: Not recorded; not opened.
limits: Not opened; numbers deliberately not stated.
agent_relevance: Letting the model try an action and read the result (run the code) is a thinking move, not just output.

source: Parasuraman & Manzey (2010) Complacency and bias in human use of automation; Goddard et al. (2012) automation bias review
finding: Users of automated aids over-rely on them, commit errors by following wrong advice, and miss events the aid does not flag. Training and showing aid reliability reduce it, but not fully. Recalled, not opened (search budget ran out).
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not opened; no figures stated.
agent_relevance: Same risk inside our loop: the model may trust a tool or checker output that is wrong. Checks must be tested, and a passing check must not be treated as proof (G3).
